records.story: The Domecq house of Jerez de la Frontera made its name with sherry, and by the account the brand gives it was in 1874 that it first sold a brandy under the name Fundador, the founder. The house calls it the first Brandy de Jerez. It was aged as sherry is aged: by criaderas and solera, rows of casks through which younger spirit is moved by stages towards the solera itself, so that every bottling is drawn from a blend of many ages. The three grades of Brandy de Jerez, Solera, Solera Reserva and Solera Gran Reserva, are each set by an average age drawn from such a system. The Domecq business changed hands more than once over the next century, and in 2016 the Philippine brandy maker Emperador completed its purchase of Bodegas Fundador, the Jerez cellars that make the brandy, from Beam Suntory. Behind a bar Fundador is where Spanish brandy begins: young, sherried and easy, and the bottle to reach for when a guest asks plainly for a Spanish brandy.

records.story: Sánchez Romate dates itself to 1781, when a Spanish merchant founded the business in Jerez de la Frontera, and it grew as a sherry house. In 1887, by the house's own account, the fourth generation of the family made a brandy for themselves and a close circle of friends, aged through a solera of sherry casks. They named it for Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza (died 1495), archbishop of Toledo from 1482, chancellor of Castile under Isabella and Ferdinand, who was called in his day the third king of Spain. What began as a family bottle became, as the house puts it, its flagship: the Cardenal Mendoza Solera Gran Reserva, labelled Clásico beside the older Carta Real. It is made from holandas, by the house's account, and aged by criaderas and solera in American oak casks seasoned with oloroso and Pedro Ximénez, and the house gives it an average of fifteen years, five times the three the rules ask of the grade. For a bartender it is the old style of Brandy de Jerez in one bottle: dark, raisined and long, the Spanish brandy to offer after dinner.

records.story: González Byass dates itself to 1835, when a young merchant founded a sherry house in Jerez de la Frontera; an English agent, whose name the house carries, later became his partner. Its fino, Tío Pepe, named for the founder's uncle, carried the house abroad. In 1951, by the house's own account, González Byass launched Lepanto as its senior brandy. Lepanto is distilled at the house's Los Arcos bodega in Jerez, twice, in two Charentais copper pot stills of the kind used in Cognac, and from Palomino wine alone, the grape of sherry; the house describes it as made wholly in Jerez, from the still to the bottle. It then ages by criaderas and solera in American oak casks that first held Tío Pepe and then oloroso, for an average of twelve years. The range grew around it: an OV, finished in casks of old oloroso, and a PX, finished in casks of Pedro Ximénez, both given fifteen years. For a bartender Lepanto is the lesson that Brandy de Jerez can be distilled where it ages, from the grape of sherry itself.

records.story: Osborne dates itself to 1772, the year of a merchants' partnership in Cádiz that the English merchant who founded the Osborne name later joined; the house came to stand at El Puerto de Santa María, the sherry town across the bay. Carlos I is older than its tie to Osborne. The brand dates its solera to 1889, and a brand story, told as a story, has a cellar master in Jerez find forgotten casks in a corner of his bodega and name the brandy they held Carlos I. In 2008 Osborne bought the Carlos I label from Pernod Ricard España, with Carlos I Imperial, Carlos III and Felipe II, as the Spanish competition authority's file of that year records. The solera is worked in American oak casks that once held sherry, sixteen scales deep by Osborne's own report, so that the brandy drawn has an average age of about twelve years. Beside it stand the Imperial XO and the 1520, which joins three Gran Reserva soleras of the house. For a bartender Carlos I is the lesson in what Solera Gran Reserva means: years of sherried oak counted as an average, here twelve where the rules ask three.

records.table: Gran Duque d'Alba is the Solera Gran Reserva of Williams & Humbert in Jerez, first made in 1945 from Palomino and Airén wine and aged in casks that held oloroso. Vanilla, cocoa and raisined fruit over toasted wood: pour it neat after dinner.
records.story: Williams & Humbert was founded in Jerez de la Frontera in 1877 by two British partners, whose names it carries, and it made its name with sherry, Dry Sack among it. Its brandy came in 1945. The house's agent in Madrid, as the brand tells it, was a friend of the Duke of Alba of the day, and asked leave to use his name; the duke proposed an ancestor instead, the third Duke of Alba, the Great Duke, a general of the sixteenth century, and the brandy carries his title. The brandy is made from young wines of Palomino and Airén grapes, distilled in pot stills, then aged by criaderas and solera in American oak casks that once held oloroso, for an average of twelve years by the house's account. An older XO stands beside it. Its bottle of 1973 was the work of a ceramicist, by the house's account, and the house's own pages spell the name de Alba where its American importer prints d'Alba. For a bartender it is the dark, raisined Gran Reserva to set beside Cardenal Mendoza when a guest wants a Spanish brandy after dinner.

others.name: Gran Duque d'Alba XO
others.note: An older solera of the house, sold beside the Solera Gran Reserva.

traps: Twelve years is an average across the solera, not an age statement, and the house's own pages give ten as well as twelve.
The duke of the name is the third Duke of Alba, of the sixteenth century, not the duke whose friendship led to it in 1945.
Gran Duque d'Alba and Gran Duque de Alba are one brandy: the house and its importers print both spellings.

cards.prompt: Which two grapes make Gran Duque d'Alba Solera Gran Reserva?
cards.answer: Palomino and Airén, made into young wines and distilled in pot stills, then aged in casks that held oloroso.

cards.prompt: Whom does the name Gran Duque d'Alba honour?
cards.answer: The third Duke of Alba, a sixteenth century general; the brandy was first made in 1945.

quiz.q: A guest asks which sherry seasoned the casks of Gran Duque d'Alba. What do you say?
quiz.explain: The bodega ages it in American oak casks that held oloroso, which gives the raisined fruit; fino and manzanilla season the casks of other houses' brandies.

quiz.q: In which year did Williams & Humbert first make Gran Duque d'Alba?
quiz.explain: 1945, by the house's account; 1877 is the year Williams & Humbert itself was founded.

report: The plan's note on age is settled from the bodega's own page: twelve years in casks that held oloroso; The Whisky Exchange gives ten, and the record says so in a trap.
The plan's note on an American importer: Palm Bay International lists the brandy in its spirits range, so it is imported; the record names no importer, since that can change.
Ownership, from the plan's note: one search summary says the bodega belongs to the Medina family; the record names no owner and no member of the family.

The two founders of 1877 (Sir Alexander Williams and Arthur Humbert on the house's page) and the seventeenth Duke of Alba whose friendship gave the name are described, not named: I did not find their dates in two sources. The third duke is described by his title, not named, for the same reason.
A news page of the house on a new look for the label was seen in a search listing and not read; the record leaves the label's history out.
Left out for want of a source: where the wine is distilled, and the age of the XO.
The Ledger holds nothing on Gran Duque d'Alba or Brandy de Jerez, so there is nothing to disagree with.
